title: Leave me alone
hookLine: a ghazal said to be his last, telling his son to go and sleep and leave him (Divan)
tomorrow: Rumi in English is missing something you can only hear. what?

lines: A POEM SAID TO BE HIS LAST.
cards: It's past three in the morning, and Inés is still rearranging the slideshow for her grandmother's memorial. One more photo, one more song. Zoe has been on the phone with her for an hour.

So, yesterday's question: what did Rumi tell his son on the night he was dying? A poem in his Divan, said to be his last, begins in a room like that one: someone awake too long beside a person they love.

teach.b: Tradition says Rumi lay dying in Konya, and his son Sultan Walad wouldn't leave his side, worn out from nights of watching. The father's answer was a ghazal.

teach.h: GO, LAY YOUR HEAD ON THE PILLOW.
teach.b: Go, lay your head on the pillow, it begins. Leave me alone. Leave me, the ruined one, who wanders all night.
He isn't pushing his son away. He's sending him to rest, because this night belongs to someone else. Here's what his followers made of it, and it's a real teaching of his path.
The Mevlevis have their own name for the night Rumi died, and it isn't a word for death.
They call it Sheb-i Arus, his wedding night: the night the lover met the Beloved, God. They mark it with music and the turning sama, not with mourning alone.
So his last request has two sides.
To his son: go and sleep; your watching can't carry me where I'm going. For himself: this night isn't an ending to guard against. It's a meeting.
One to tell a friend tonight: in Rumi's tradition, a death can be called a wedding. And for anyone keeping a vigil, the line gives quiet permission. Rest is not leaving.

how: Mevlevis mark the anniversary of Rumi's death as Sheb-i Arus, his wedding night, with music, recitation and the sama ceremony. The ghazal 'go, lay your head on the pillow' is read in Persian as his farewell.

o: Rumi's words sending his tired son off to rest
a Sufi vow of silence before a long fast
Rumi's angry reply to his critics in Konya

games.q: the last night: tap the pairs.
p: the son who wouldn't leave his side
the city where Rumi lived and died

s: in this ghazal, 'leave me alone' is Rumi pushing his son away
he sends a worn-out son to rest. the night, he says, belongs to someone else.
Mevlevis call the night Rumi died his wedding night
Sheb-i Arus: the night the lover met the Beloved, marked with music and sama.
we know for certain this was the last poem Rumi wrote
tradition says it's his last. that's a tradition, not a dated record.

games.q: a friend has sat up night after night with her dying father. she asks whether going home to sleep would be wrong. what fits Rumi's last ghazal?
o: go and sleep; love doesn't need you awake every hour.
stay; a good child never leaves the room.
say goodbye now and stop coming; it's easier.
games.why: Rumi sent his own watching son to bed: go, lay your head on the pillow. rest is not leaving.

practice: Rest your head the way you would on a pillow: lean back, or fold your arms on the table and lay your head on them. Feel the weight leave your neck and shoulders. For these two minutes, let someone else keep the watch.

wordCard.voice: Leave me alone: Rumi's request to his tired son. Not a door slammed, but a blessing: go and sleep.

orig.note: Persian: wedding night. The Mevlevis' name for the night Rumi died; in Turkish, Şeb-i Arus.

carryVoice: Your line: go and sleep. The watch can be handed back. Six days with Rumi again.

sources.ref: Divan-i Shams, the ghazal 'ro sar beneh be balin, tanha mara reha kon' (go, lay your head on the pillow, leave me alone), traditionally his last
Aflaki, Manaqib al-'arifin (accounts of Rumi's last days and Sultan Walad), and Franklin Lewis, Rumi: Past and Present, East and West (2000)
